content: Which stable versions of Lean 4 are known to contain soundness bugs?
None?
Was the bug that @Mario Carneiro found fixed in older releases?
https://leanprover.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/270676-lean4/topic/Soundness.20bug.3A.20hasLooseBVars.20is.20not.20conservative/near/521286338
Is it possible to tag LeanFRO in my post? They must know the answer.
The Lean FRO is reading this channel, so you don't need to additionally tag them.

The FRO doesn't really track this kind of thing either. The two fixes for soundness issues after the release of 4.0.0 that I remember are lean4#8060 and lean4#8559 / lean4#8560, both of which fix issues which had been around for ~forever, so presumably the answer is that any version which does not have these commits (or backported versions of them) has a proof of False.
Thanks for the reply! Can you please make a table of which stable Lean 4 versions are known to prove False? Such an essential information should be readily available.

We might make such a table once we enter the business of supporting old Lean versions under some kind of LTS model or if soundness bugs become more common than one every few years on average. For now, you can just make the table yourself, it shouldn't be difficult.

Well, I can start tracking soundness issues myself, but I am sure that other users and stakeholders would prefer to see an authoritative answer from Lean FRO rather than from a random dude with crooked teeth from eastern Europe.

Honestly, I find it alarming that such crucial information is not written on the Lean FRO website.

The FRO's (perhaps implicit) policy has been that there are almost no backports of any fixes to older versions anyway - you need to upgrade to the current version. In that light, I find the policy reasonable.

I agree that a list of soundness bugs, or even long-term support, are nice to have --- but the FRO's time is limited. I'd rather have it spend its time on other things.
Also: if you make such a table, adopting it on the FRO's webpage is much easier than if they have to compile it themselves. Be the change you want to see :-)

With my moderator hat on:

I find it alarming that such crucial information is not written on the Lean FRO website.

is very strong language. I understand why you feel this way. The thing is: non-subtle posts can make it really hard to be empathetic with each other, and empathy is what we need (especially for challenging discussions). (My personal favourite take on this is by Aaron Turon, in the context of the Rust project.)
Noted. I will refrain from writing such sentences next time.

Michael Rothgang said:

Also: if you make such a table, adopting it on the FRO's webpage is much easier than if they have to compile it themselves. Be the change you want to see :-)

It took me less than 3 hours to compile.

The following repository lists all unsound stable Lean 4 versions that I know of:
https://github.com/madvorak/lean4-soundness
To the best of my knowledge, all other stable Lean 4 versions should be sound.

Please let me know if there is a known soundness bug in a newer Lean version than listed!

Michael Rothgang said:

there are almost no backports of any fixes to older versions anyway

Is it something that the community could do? I don't imagine it being done on large scale — only backporting bugfixes for critical errors to all stable versions impacted by those critical errors.

If you are going to document soundness bugs, I would suggest you structure it more like https://github.com/rocq-prover/Rocq/blob/master/dev/doc/critical-bugs.md - Describe what the bug was, link to a PR/issue, and say which stable versions or RCs were affected.

Ultimately, we need two different documents:
(1) The more important document, general-public-facing document, which provides the crucial one bit of information about every stable Lean version. This document will be needed whenever a reviewer gets a paper formalized in Lean.
(2) Another document, developers-facing document, which distinguishes which bug affects which version. This document will be needed if we start fixing bugs in older releases (and then, according to the latter document, the former document will be updated).
It could be said that (2) will subsume (1), but we will nevertheless need to keep preserving and updating (1) for the information about soundness to be retrieved in constant time.

Mario Carneiro said:

https://github.com/rocq-prover/Rocq/blob/master/dev/doc/critical-bugs.md

Note that I, as person who doesn't know much about Rocq, am unable to retrieve (in a reasonable time) the information about which version of Rocq is trustworty.

As a person who does not know much about rocq, are you in a reasonable position to check that an artifact actually states what its author claims? This is a far more likely mistake than exploiting a kernel bug.
Probably yes, but I shouldn't be trusted. I'd rather ask a Rocq expert to check it for me.

Let me try to make some stone soup: I have a draft version for (2) --- i.e., (my attempt at) a full list of critical or soundness bugs in Lean 4, describing the nature of the bug, the impact and affected versions. Naturally, such information should be checked very carefully, and I cannot do this alone. Would an FRO expert (e.g. @Julia Markus Himmel) like to help me review it? If so, I'm very happy to PR it to the FRO's webpage afterwards.
I'm happy to review it and check against my recollection
DMed you the current draft
My current draft (with a few more bugs added by Mario) is now at https://github.com/grunweg/lean-critical-bugs. Critical review is very welcome!

A few quick ones:

  • [2] should also be caught by nanoda given that it has a completely different loose bvars mechanism as far as I understand
  • I think doing the list as bullet points instead of with bold text interspersed might help readability?
  • the link for my fix for the prim read issue is broken: https://github.com/grunweg/lean-critical-bugs/blob/main/lean4#13392

A more general note regarding prim read, if you want to include the phenomenon of "Software that is verified in lean to be correct will still have vulnerabilities" as a critical bug you would basically have to list all correctness fixes we make to the runtime as a critical bug. It also opens the question whether you would e.g. consider a DoS attack a vulnerability in which case even trivial things like crashing the runtime or having memleaks is a vulnerability. Which is to say, where do you draw the line for critical. These kinds of considerations are also why the Linux kernel initially refused to hand out CVEs for itself because basically any bug in the kernel is a security vulnerability (and now are in this mess https://lore.kernel.org/linux-cve-announce/). Similarly any bug in the runtime can be considered a security vulnerability from some angle.
I think we should include correctness fixes to the runtime, but under a separate category
certainly anything that allows lean to segfault should be included

Mario Carneiro said:

certainly anything that allows lean to segfault should be included

Do you mean segfaults or crashes in general here?
segfaults (or other UB) specifically
as those are the most weaponizable into soundness bugs or straight CVEs
panics aren't really the same category of severity

Thanks for the feedback! I will split out runtime bugs into a separate category, fix the data for [2] and tweak the formatting. I'll happily take further runtime bugs to list; I don't feel like compiling that list also.
